newsitem.title: ITALY: Israel's Peres worried about peace - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Peres worried about peace - newspaper.

text.p: Former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres said in a newspaper interview published on Monday that he was worried about the future of the Middle East peace process and said he hoped the region would not see war again.

Asked by an interviewer in Tel Aviv for the Italian daily La Stampa whether he felt the peace process was in danger, Peres answered: "Certainly yes, after the elections we are like a boat left without oars in the middle of a lake".
Peres, the Labour Party leader, was referring to Israeli elections in May when he was ousted as prime minister by Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu.
He declined to give his opinion of Netanyahu. "On that point, I don't want to say a single word," Peres said.
But he did say that Israel was without a "politics of peace...and I can only hope that the absence of these politics does not help bring about another war".
Peres said obstacles to peace included "the new settlements, the problems of Hebron and the absence of true negotiations with Lebanon and Syria".
Asked whether he thought a fresh war was possible, Peres said: "In the absence of a politics of peace, anything is possible. Also terrorism is not a minor thing".
Before his election, the right-wing Netanyahu vowed never to meet Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat if he became prime minister. Under U.S. pressure, he met Arafat on September 4.
Peres noted that some aspects of the peace process were going forward. Talks on implementing peace deals are due to resume next week.
"In part they are blocked, but in part they are going forward because, notwithstanding everything, their power is great," he said.

"The PLO and Arafat were recognised, the Palestinian administration is established in Gaza and the West Bank, there were important economic conferences at Casablanca and Amman and there was an anti-terrorism conference at Sharm el-Sheikh," he said. "This has created a strong and varied front. These are immovable milestones for peace."

Peres, who announced last week that he would not run for prime minister in Israel's next scheduled elections in the year 2000, said he still mourned Labour Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated by a right-wing Jew last November.
"It's enough to say that we were like two parts of a whole. I am missing half of my body. What more can I say ?," Peres said.
